title: Polarisation as evidence of transverse waves

evidence.evidence_gap: Dependency retrieval is based on the verified Lesson 12 handoff.

hints: Recall the short region sequence around the colours seen by the eye.
walkthrough: In the electromagnetic spectrum, visible light lies between infrared and ultraviolet.
Electromagnetic waves, including visible light, are transverse.

ai_rubric.observable: Names visible light as the region between infrared and ultraviolet.
States that visible-light waves are transverse.

hints: Separate the direction of travel from the direction of oscillation.
walkthrough: Plane polarisation acts on transverse oscillations.
It restricts them to one direction perpendicular to propagation, so option B is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects option B.

hints: The oscillation direction need not match energy transfer.
walkthrough: The statement explicitly says that the wave travels east.
Vertical describes its oscillation, so energy transfer is east and option A is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects option A.

hints: Compare oscillation direction with propagation direction.
walkthrough: A longitudinal wave oscillates parallel to propagation.
There is no transverse oscillation direction for the filter to select, so option C is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects option C.

hints: Read travel and oscillation as separate directions.
walkthrough: The wave travels horizontally towards the detector, so that is the energy-transfer direction.
The stated oscillation is vertical.

ai_rubric.observable: States that energy transfer is horizontal towards the detector.
States that the oscillation direction is vertical.

hints: The transmission axis should match the allowed oscillation.
walkthrough: The filter is aligned when its transmission axis follows the wave's oscillation direction.
Draw the axis vertically and explain that it matches the vertical oscillation.

ai_rubric.observable: Draws a vertical transmission axis on the filter.
Explains that the axis is aligned with the vertical oscillation direction.

hints: Name both the restricted quantity and its relation to travel.
walkthrough: The polarising filter acts on oscillation direction, not propagation direction.
The transmitted oscillation is restricted to one direction perpendicular to propagation.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the filter restricts the oscillation direction.
States that the selected direction is perpendicular to propagation.

hints: Ask what kind of wave offers different oscillation directions perpendicular to travel.
walkthrough: A transverse wave has oscillations perpendicular to propagation.
Different directions are available in that transverse plane, and turning the filter changes which component is selected.
The signal therefore depends on filter orientation, which is evidence of transverse oscillations.

ai_rubric.observable: States that a transverse wave oscillates perpendicular to its direction of travel.
Explains that rotating the filter changes which transverse oscillation direction or component is selected.
Concludes that the rotation-dependent signal is evidence that the wave is transverse.

hints: Use perpendicular for light and parallel for sound.
walkthrough: Draw the light oscillation perpendicular to left-to-right travel, for example vertically.
Draw sound-particle arrows left and right, parallel to travel.

ai_rubric.observable: Adds a light oscillation arrow perpendicular to the direction of travel.
Adds sound-particle motion arrows parallel to the direction of travel.

hints: Use the registered wording before applying it.
walkthrough: A transverse wave is a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
The light oscillation is perpendicular to its left-to-right energy transfer, so it is transverse.

ai_rubric.observable: States the accepted definition: a transverse wave is a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
Applies the perpendicular relationship to classify the light wave as transverse.

hints: Compare whether a rotating filter has a transverse direction to select.
walkthrough: For light, a rotated filter changes the transverse direction or component that is selected.
For sound, particle motion is along the travel direction, so rotating around that direction cannot select a transverse oscillation.
Thus light can be plane polarised, while sound in air cannot be plane polarised in this sense.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that rotating the filter changes the transverse oscillation direction selected from the light wave.
Explains that sound motion is parallel to travel, so no transverse direction can be selected and sound cannot be plane polarised in this sense.

originality_scope_evidence_audit.evidence_gap_note: Primary P2 evidence is qualitative. Original radio-detector and laboratory contexts assess the same controlled demand without reproducing official wording, numbers or diagrams.
originality_scope_evidence_audit.scope_note: Malus's law, quantitative filter transmission and the unpolarised first-filter intensity calculation are deferred.
